title: Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.
summary: The majority limited recovery for unperformed mine-restoration work to the farm’s $300 diminution in value because it treated restoration as incidental to the lease and its cost as grossly disproportionate to its economic benefit.
notes: The notes report Schneberger’s later adherence to Peevyhouse and present competing readings of economic waste. The separately assigned lease is in the Contracts Selections (PDF page 699; retyped at page 703), linked below.

sections.Parties: Willie and Lucille Peevyhouse owned the farm and leased it for coal extraction. Garland Coal & Mining Company was the lessee that performed the mining but failed to complete the promised restoration.
sections.Material Facts:
The Peevyhouses granted a five-year strip-mining lease in 1954. Garland agreed both to the ordinary mining terms and to specified restorative work at the end of the lease. The work would require moving many thousands of cubic yards of dirt and cost approximately $29,000. Evidence placed the increase in the farm’s market value from that work at only $300. The Peevyhouses sued for $25,000.

The significance of the restoration promise was contested in the opinions. The majority described it as incidental to profitable coal extraction. Justice Irwin’s dissent emphasized Garland’s admission that the owners had insisted on the restoration provisions and would not have agreed to the lease without them. Whether restoration was central or incidental is therefore a contested characterization, not an uncontested fact.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment on a $5,000 jury verdict. Both sides appealed. The Oklahoma Supreme Court reduced the judgment to $300 and affirmed it as modified, by a divided vote. The casebook identifies the decision as 1963 and reports its citation as 1962 OK 267, 382 P.2d 109.
sections.Issue: Does expectation compensation for a breached restoration clause equal the cost of completing the work, or may it be limited to the much smaller increase in property value?
sections.Holding: The majority stated that reasonable cost of performance ordinarily governs. It applied an exception where the breached provision was merely incidental to the contract’s main purpose and the economic benefit of performance was grossly disproportionate to its cost. Recovery was therefore limited to $300.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority distinguished Groves by characterizing the main transaction as a mining arrangement rather than a contract whose principal object was grading or construction. It also drew on authorities comparing completion costs with the benefit to be obtained. Although restoration would not require demolishing a completed building, the majority considered the disproportion between expenditure and economic benefit sufficient under its chosen formulation.

This reasoning makes characterization decisive: calling restoration incidental narrows the protected expectation even though the clause was expressly included. The dissent’s account of bargaining shows the difficulty of equating an improvement’s market value with the owners’ contractual interest. The holding therefore belongs beside the contrary Groves approach and the narrower destructive-repair reasoning in Plante and Jacob & Youngs.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Peevyhouse connects contractual purpose and bargaining evidence to the measure of damages. Its facts show why a complete remedies analysis must distinguish market value, personal value, and the performance expressly purchased.

topics.remedies: Applies an incidental-obligation and gross-disproportionality limitation on restoration damages.
topics.assent: The dissent uses the owners’ actual insistence on a term to contest the majority’s account of the bargain.
topics.interpretation: The majority and dissent disagree about how to identify the agreement’s central purpose.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Irwin would have awarded the cost of performance. He argued that the owners specifically bargained for restoration and that a smaller award effectively rewrote their agreement for the breaching company’s benefit.
